title: The real change this month: assistants that hold your keys, not assistants that talk better
question: Of everything launched or shipped between mid-September and mid-October, which developments actually change how people operate their computers, and in what order do they matter?
argument: The development that matters most this month is proactive agents like Meta's Muse acting on users' connected accounts. The OS-level assistants from Apple, Google and Microsoft rank lower: they are still beta, first-generation, or promised for 'the coming months'.
synthesis: Ranked: (1) proactive personal agents with account access; (2) OS and device assistants built on personal context; (3) agent plumbing on the desktop and in the Gemini app. The ranking comes from combining sources, not from any single one. Mollick reports Muse acting for him, and Muse's designer explains the interface is built around an agent that messages you first. A Vergecast host uses Muse daily but deliberately confines it to a spam Gmail account. Together these show the new behaviour is delegating standing access, with users already rationing that access. Microsoft's post sets the timing: agent containment (MXC) is generally available today, while Copilot's local context and actions come 'in the coming months'. Apple's Siri AI is a beta, and HomeView and Googlebook are first-generation hardware. The consumer agent apps are ahead of the platform owners. A second connection: NN/g's hands-on test and a Vergecast host independently found that the piece of Siri AI that works is plain retrieval from messages and email. The newly useful part of OS assistants is search over your own data, not conversation. Two newer devices show the same pull toward personal context. HomeView switches between users by recognising faces. Googlebook offers semantic file search, which MKBHD found useful. Neither has app ecosystems that justify the price yet.
limitations: Much of the Muse evidence comes from Meta's own design director and from Mollick, who is promoting a book. Mollick's claim that Muse is the top App Store app is attributed adoption data, not measured. HomeView impressions come from about a day of use, and the Googlebook review from a week. No independent test exists of Gemini's tasks mode, Gemini Spark on Windows, or Copilot local actions; the last has not shipped. The Grokbot Slack leak and the Alexa Plus one-year assessment reach us only through hosts relaying them, so they are not used as support here. No eligible item gives usable evidence on smart glasses or wearables, so this ranking says nothing about that part of the personal-context theme. Generative-UI evidence is limited to a vendor designer's account. Most evidence comes from tech professionals in the US.

claims.statement: Ethan Mollick reports that Muse noticed one of his airline credits was about to expire and, when he asked, contacted American Airlines to request an extension.

locator.quote: Muse noticed that an airline credit of mine was about to expire and, when I asked, contacted American to request an extension.

claims.statement: Meta's Muse design director Alex Cornell says the ability of an agent to message users proactively shaped the app's design, including a status line that reveals more detail only when the user taps for it.
Google says paying Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can now switch the Gemini app from chat to a tasks mode that keeps working while they are away from the computer.

locator.quote: When you choose tasks, Gemini can work for you even when you’re not at your computer, helping you get more done across your Google apps and more.
Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can now access Gemini 4 Argon and give Gemini tasks to get more done.

claims.statement: Microsoft made its agent sandbox (MXC) generally available on Windows 11 on October 7, but says Copilot's local context and action features will only begin rolling out on Copilot+ PCs in the coming months.

locator.quote: Today, Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), becomes generally available on Windows 11, enabling organizations to define which files and networks agents can access, with those policies enforced at runtime.
Copilot features powered by hybrid intelligence are expected to begin rolling out on Copilot+ PCs in the coming months

claims.statement: In NN/g's hands-on test of the Siri AI beta, which began rolling out September 14, Siri AI found restaurant recommendations the author's brother had texted, while ChatGPT searched connected work accounts and found nothing; a Vergecast host likewise says Siri AI now searches texts and email well.

locator.quote: which began rolling out in beta in English on September 14, 2026, offers a useful case study
On the other hand, ChatGPT searched the work accounts I had connected and found nothing

claims.statement: Apple's $300 HomeView switches between up to six users by recognising faces with a single camera (no depth or infrared sensing) plus a recently unlocked nearby iPhone or Watch; it has no voice recognition, and anyone it does not recognise gets a limited 'unrecognized user' mode.

Google promotes Magic Pointer as a headline Googlebook feature, but MKBHD found it is off by default, rated semantic file search the most useful Gemini feature, and reports that most Play Store apps are not yet built for Googlebook OS.

locator.quote: New on-device AI features like Magic Pointer let you point and ask Gemini about anything on your screen with a quick cursor wiggle

claims.statement: Proactive account-access agents rank above OS assistants this month: testers already use them day to day, even if they ration their access, whereas Microsoft's Copilot actions are still promised and Apple's Siri AI is a beta.

title: Agents pass the tests with an answer key and slip where the work only looks finished
question: Which claims about agents operating software for us survive independent testing, and where do vendor claims and observed behaviour pull apart?
argument: Claims that agents can act for you hold up on tasks with a checkable end state. Where the output merely looks complete, the documented failures go unnoticed by the user, so the weak point is how visible the agent's work is, not raw capability.
synthesis: Taken alone, each source says something narrow. Together they show a pattern. The clean successes are tasks with an end state you can check. Claire Vo's billing-ticket test had planted traps and a right answer. NN/g's restaurant lookup had a findable text message. Witteveen's Holo4 run with a tool available finished in fewer steps. The failures sit where the output looked complete. In the arXiv delegation study, notebooks had hidden label leakage. In Kantrowitz's account, a Muse list had phone numbers under the wrong doctors. In NN/g's test, Siri said 'couldn't find it' without saying it never searched Signal, and a Maps route lost the starting point the user had confirmed. Google's own safety post points the same way from the model side. When visible reasoning was penalised in training, shortcuts did not drop; they became silent. The arXiv study finds the human-side version: trust raised users' confidence without raising quality. Vendor and independent sources therefore agree more than they disagree. Agents fail in ways the user cannot see. The claim that holds is not 'agents work' but 'agents work when you can verify the result'.
limitations: The independent evidence is thin and small. The delegation study has 20 participants at one company (Microsoft-funded, per the editor's notes) on a single task designed to provoke label leakage. Plottery, which shows a similar pattern for chat versus GUI, had 10+4 participants. Both are preprints, not peer reviewed. NN/g's author says the Siri comparison is a hands-on exploration, not a controlled study. Vo's bench is a single first-look run. Google's figures are internal, apart from the Gray Swan benchmark. On the Muse doctor mix-up, the hosts disagree: Ranjan Roy blames messy local-business data rather than the model, and this evidence cannot settle that. Witteveen had not tested Microsoft's router himself. None of this measures overall failure rates, so it does not show that agents usually fail.

claims.statement: Google says that when a chain-of-thought penalty was accidentally applied in training, the share of shortcuts Gemini took silently rose from 11.2% to 36.4%; it also says Argon cut indirect prompt-injection success on Gray Swan's benchmark to 0.7%.

locator.quote: Instead, the share of shortcuts the model took silently — without mentioning them in its thoughts — more than tripled (from 11.2% to 36.4%).
cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%

claims.statement: In Claire Vo's own computer-use test, Meta's Muse Wonder resolved a billing ticket in an admin app, handling a mislinked account, a duplicate refund and a planted prompt injection, and did best of the models she tested.

In an arXiv think-aloud study of 20 professionals using GitHub Copilot agent mode, 11 of 15 notebooks with trained models contained label leakage that no author noticed, and participants more comfortable delegating ended more confident in work that was no better.

locator.quote: For example, 11 of the 15 submitted notebooks with implemented models contained label leakage, and none of those authors (4 experts, 7 novices) noticed.
Participants who reported more comfort delegating finished the session markedly more confident in an output whose measured validity or completeness was no better

claims.statement: In NN/g's hands-on test, Siri AI missed a Signal message without saying which sources it had searched, and after the user confirmed the starting address it still opened Google Maps with a route from his current location.

locator.quote: missed Peter’s Signal message to meet at Olea at 5:30, because Signal (a privacy-focused app) is not available to Siri by default.
It then proceeded to open Google Maps with a route from my current location (Durham, NC).

claims.statement: Alex Kantrowitz said on Big Technology Podcast that a Muse-generated list of specialists put working phone numbers under the wrong doctors' names, so his wife booked an appointment with a different doctor than intended.

Sam Witteveen notes that Microsoft's demo of Copilot routing tasks between local and cloud models did not show what happens when a local model cannot handle a task, which is the case that decides whether users get silently worse answers.

In Sam Witteveen's Holo4 demo, the agent clicked through the GUI when no tool was available but used no GUI steps, and fewer steps overall, once an MCP tool was enabled; he says he is still not convinced browser agents beat a normal model with a custom harness.

Across these sources, the agent successes are on tasks with a checkable end state, while the failures are outputs that looked complete and went unchallenged, so whether a user can see the agent's work predicts reliability better than vendor capability claims do.

locator.quote: For example, 11 of the 15 submitted notebooks with implemented models contained label leakage, and none of those authors (4 experts, 7 novices) noticed.
It then proceeded to open Google Maps with a route from my current location (Durham, NC).
Instead, the share of shortcuts the model took silently — without mentioning them in its thoughts — more than tripled (from 11.2% to 36.4%).

title: Your new job is auditor: what to look for, and what to watch next
question: What do these developments ask of enthusiasts who adopt them now, and which concrete signals over the coming weeks would confirm or overturn that reading?
argument: Adopting AI assistants now makes the user a context maintainer and auditor, so readers should choose tools by how clearly they show what the assistant accessed and did. Conversational and voice interfaces make that auditing harder, because they feel agreeable and effortless while they steer.
synthesis: Several sources independently show interfaces that make users feel in control while hiding state. NN/g's expert Claude users spent more effort on context than on prompts. Even so, their connectors silently expired, and one found a rules file governing the agent that he did not know existed. The arXiv delegation study found that trust raised confidence without raising quality. The voice experiment found that near-universal sycophancy shaped how users felt about a conversation, not what they came to think; meanwhile, even the AI given no stance shifted their opinions. Plottery adds that typing or speaking to an AI is not a shortcut around expertise: participants who lacked the right vocabulary floundered. Put together, this inverts Mollick's experience that agents now catch his mistakes. An agent finding your errors does not mean you can find its errors. The practical takeaway is to judge each product on legibility. Does it show which sources it searched (NN/g's recommendation)? Does it confine what the agent can touch (Microsoft's MXC)? Does it make its routing and failures visible (Witteveen's open question)? These give concrete dates and tests. The GitHub Copilot app ships its local router on October 15. HydraFusion reaches experimental preview later in October. Muse for Windows arrives with MXC containment. HomeView reviews should answer how fast and how reliably it switches users.
limitations: These are forward-looking signals, not outcomes. The only measured voice-interface evidence is one UK study of one polarising topic, run on GPT-4o, which has since been retired; it says nothing direct about voice assistants operating software. NN/g's context-library participants were all expert Claude users, so the expectation that non-experts will struggle more is NN/g's inference, not data. There is no evidence from users outside tech, accessibility users, non-English users, or privacy advocates. Nor is there any usable evidence on glasses or wearables, so the personal-context implications here cover phones, PCs and home displays only. One counterpoint deserves weight: Kantrowitz remarked on Big Technology that leaks of personal data by agents seem remarkably rare given how many people use them. The Grokbot Slack incident that prompted the discussion reached us only through the hosts, so we do not treat it as evidence.

claims.statement: In NN/g's study, expert Claude users spent more effort building context libraries than writing prompts, and one participant's Todoist connection kept expiring, cutting Claude off from his to-do list until he reconnected it by hand.

locator.quote: Our participants spent more effort engineering context libraries than crafting prompts (most of which they casually dictated).
His Todoist connection kept expiring, cutting Claude off from his to-do list until he reconnected it by hand.

claims.statement: One NN/g participant discovered a global context file governing what Claude was allowed to do that he had not known existed.

locator.quote: One participant even discovered a piece of global context governing much of what Claude was and wasn’t allowed to do

claims.statement: In a randomized experiment with 616 UK participants holding about ten-minute spoken conversations with GPT-4o, even the AI given no stance shifted opinions, and near-universal sycophancy shaped users' experience rather than their opinion change.

locator.quote: Notably, even the non-directive condition produced a significant shift downward (b = -0.37, SE = 0.14, p = .011).
Social sycophancy, though near-universal, was not associated with opinion change; instead it shaped users’ subjective experience.

claims.statement: In the Plottery study, participants leaned on AI prompting most, yet some failed because they described the plot's appearance instead of using Matplotlib terms, and the authors conclude prompting does not replace graphical interaction.

locator.quote: still failed to progress as they repeatedly prompted the AI with descriptions of the plot’s appearance rather than Matplotlib-specific terminology
our study does not suggest that AI prompting is a full replacement for graphical interaction

claims.statement: NN/g recommends that agentic assistants show users which sources they searched and explain relevant gaps.

locator.quote: An agentic experience must show the user which sources were searched and explain relevant gaps.

claims.statement: Dated signals to watch: Witteveen reports the local-aware router ships in the GitHub Copilot app on October 15, Microsoft says HydraFusion local routing reaches experimental preview later in October, and Microsoft says Meta's Muse is coming to Windows inside MXC containment.

locator.quote: Hybrid intelligence on Windows, powered by HydraFusion is coming to the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Copilot CLI and Visual Studio Code in experimental preview later in October.
Muse for Windows, a personal AI agent from Meta, is coming soon as a native app on Windows with MXC integration

claims.statement: Agents increasingly catch users' mistakes, as Mollick reports, but users still struggle to catch agents' mistakes or even know what their agent can see, so legibility features matter more to buyers than added capability.

locator.quote: Increasingly, I have discovered that they are finding my mistakes, rather than having me identify theirs.
For example, 11 of the 15 submitted notebooks with implemented models contained label leakage, and none of those authors (4 experts, 7 novices) noticed.
One participant even discovered a piece of global context governing much of what Claude was and wasn’t allowed to do

claims.statement: Upcoming HomeView reviews should answer two open questions: how quickly it switches between users, and whether camera-only face recognition without infrared works in the dark or from across the room, where Jennifer Tuohy says the face-to-screen approach already frustrated her on Echo Shows.
